lessons.title: Animal, plant and bacterial cells
lessons.summary: Nuclei contain genetic material; ribosomes make proteins; mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Nuclei contain genetic material; ribosomes make proteins; mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration. Cytoplasm supports many reactions and membranes control movement. Photosynthetic plant cells also have chloroplasts, cellulose walls and a permanent vacuole.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Bacteria have a membrane, wall, cytoplasm and ribosomes but no nucleus. Their main DNA forms a loop; plasmids are extra DNA rings. Underground root hair cells normally lack chloroplasts, so do not draw every plant cell as a photosynthetic leaf cell.

keypoints: Nuclei contain genetic material; ribosomes make proteins; mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration.
Bacteria have a membrane, wall, cytoplasm and ribosomes but no nucleus.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: Which structure makes proteins?

exam.q: Explain three differences between a typical photosynthetic plant cell and a bacterial cell.
ms: Plant DNA is enclosed in a nucleus; bacterial DNA is not.
The plant cell has chloroplasts; the bacterium does not.
The plant cell has a permanent vacuole; the bacterium does not.

lessons.title: Microscopy and magnification
lessons.summary: Magnification enlarges an image; resolution distinguishes close points.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Magnification enlarges an image; resolution distinguishes close points. Electron microscopes reveal finer detail than light microscopes because they have greater resolution as well as greater magnification. Enlarging a blurry image does not reveal new detail.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. Convert units before dividing: 1 mm = 1000 μm. A 36 mm image representing a 12 μm cell has magnification 36000 ÷ 12 = 3000. Magnification has no unit.

keypoints: Magnification enlarges an image; resolution distinguishes close points.
Magnification = image size ÷ actual size.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: A 20 μm cell appears 40 mm long. Calculate magnification.
What distinguishes two close organelles?

exam.q: A cell image is 54 mm wide at ×1800. Calculate actual width in micrometres.
ms: Actual size = image size / magnification.

practical.title: Required practical 1 · Light microscopy
method: Place a thin plant tissue layer on a slide, add suitable stain and lower a coverslip at an angle.
Start on low power and focus with coarse then fine adjustment; increase power as appropriate.
Observe plant and prepared animal cells; make clear proportional labelled drawings with a scale or magnification.
variables: Keep specimen thickness and illumination suitable.
Record eyepiece and objective magnifications.
safety: Handle glass slides carefully.
Avoid stain contact and follow school eye-protection guidance.
practical.analysis: Use image size divided by magnification for actual size, with consistent units. Total microscope magnification equals eyepiece × objective.

lessons.title: Specialisation and differentiation
lessons.summary: Differentiation develops specialised structures.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Differentiation develops specialised structures. Most animal cells differentiate early; many plant cells retain this ability throughout life. Mature animal cell division mainly supports repair and replacement. Explain why a feature suits a task rather than merely listing features.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Sperm have a tail for swimming and many mitochondria. Nerve cells have long extensions for impulse transmission; muscle cells have contractile proteins. Root hairs enlarge absorbing area. Hollow lignified xylem conducts water; living phloem transports sugars.

keypoints: Differentiation develops specialised structures.
Sperm have a tail for swimming and many mitochondria.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

exam.q: Explain three adaptations of a sperm cell for fertilisation.
ms: A tail allows movement towards an egg.
Many mitochondria support respiration for movement.
Enzymes in the head help penetrate egg coverings.

lessons.title: Mitosis and the cell cycle
lessons.summary: Chromosomes contain DNA and many genes; body cells normally have chromosome pairs.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Chromosomes contain DNA and many genes; body cells normally have chromosome pairs. Before division, a cell grows, increases its organelles and copies its DNA. These preparations give daughter cells complete genetic information and cell machinery.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: During mitosis, chromosome copies separate and nuclei divide. Cytoplasm and membrane then divide to form two genetically identical cells with the original chromosome number. Mitosis supports growth and repair, whereas meiosis forms gametes.

keypoints: Chromosomes contain DNA and many genes; body cells normally have chromosome pairs.
During mitosis, chromosome copies separate and nuclei divide.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: Three cells each complete two rounds of division. How many result?

exam.q: Describe how the cell cycle produces two genetically identical daughter cells.
ms: DNA is replicated before division.
Copies of each chromosome separate to opposite ends and nuclei divide.
Cytoplasm and membrane divide, leaving identical chromosome sets.

lessons.title: Stem cells: benefits, risks and ethics
lessons.summary: Stem cells are unspecialised cells that can divide and differentiate.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Stem cells are unspecialised cells that can divide and differentiate. Embryonic stem cells can form most human cell types; adult bone-marrow stem cells produce a more limited range, including blood cells. Plant meristems can produce different plant tissues throughout life.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Replacement cells may help damaged tissues, but infection and uncontrolled division are risks. Therapeutic cloning produces genetically matched cells, reducing rejection. Embryo use raises ethical objections. Meristems can rapidly clone rare plants or crops with desirable characteristics.

keypoints: Stem cells are unspecialised cells that can divide and differentiate.
Replacement cells may help damaged tissues, but infection and uncontrolled division are risks.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: Where are adult human stem cells found?

exam.q: Evaluate embryonic stem cells for replacing damaged nerve tissue.

lessons.title: Diffusion and exchange surfaces
lessons.summary: Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient. Higher temperature, larger area and a steeper gradient usually increase its rate. Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross cell membranes by diffusion; the process itself requires no energy from respiration.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: As size increases, surface area to volume ratio decreases. Large organisms need specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems. Alveoli and villi have large areas and short diffusion distances; blood flow and ventilation maintain gradients.

keypoints: Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient.
As size increases, surface area to volume ratio decreases.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: A cube has side 2 cm. Express its surface area to volume ratio as x:1.
Which change speeds diffusion?

exam.q: Explain why alveoli exchange gases rapidly.
ms: Many alveoli provide a large surface area.
Thin walls give a short diffusion distance.
Ventilation and blood flow maintain concentration gradients.

lessons.title: Osmosis and percentage mass change
lessons.summary: Osmosis is net water movement through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Osmosis is net water movement through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution. Water moves both ways, but there is a net movement when concentrations differ. Water entry can make plant cells turgid.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Percentage mass change = (final − initial mass) ÷ initial mass × 100. Changing from 2.0 g to 2.3 g gives +15%; a negative value means loss. A graph crossing zero estimates a solution concentration causing no net water movement.

keypoints: Osmosis is net water movement through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution.
Percentage mass change = (final − initial mass) ÷ initial mass × 100.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: A cylinder changes from 4.0 g to 3.6 g. Calculate percentage mass change.
When does water enter a cell by osmosis?
opts: Outside is more dilute than inside
checks.why: Outside is more dilute than inside

exam.q: Explain why potato tissue loses mass in concentrated sugar solution.
ms: The outside solution is more concentrated than the cell contents.
Water moves out by osmosis across partially permeable cell membranes.
Water loss reduces tissue mass.

practical.title: Required practical 2 · Osmosis in plant tissue
method: Cut equal potato cylinders and record initial masses.
Immerse in equal volumes of a concentration range for equal times.
Remove, blot consistently and reweigh; repeat each concentration.
variables: Independent: sugar or salt concentration.
Dependent: percentage mass change.
Control dimensions, tissue source, solution volume, temperature and time.
safety: Use cutting equipment on a suitable surface under supervision.
Do not eat laboratory samples.
practical.analysis: Calculate percentage changes and means. Plot concentration against percentage change and interpolate the zero-change concentration, recognising scatter and measurement uncertainty.

lessons.title: Active transport and comparing transport
lessons.summary: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient, from lower to higher concentration.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient, from lower to higher concentration. It requires energy from respiration. Root hairs absorb mineral ions from dilute soil solutions; intestinal cells can absorb sugars against their gradient.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Diffusion moves particles down a gradient; osmosis specifically describes water through a partially permeable membrane; active transport needs energy. Many mitochondria can support energy-demanding transport. The presence of a membrane alone does not prove osmosis: identify the substance moving.

keypoints: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient, from lower to higher concentration.
Diffusion moves particles down a gradient; osmosis specifically describes water through a partially permeable membrane; active transport needs energy.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: Which process requires energy from respiration?
Mineral concentration is lower in soil than a root cell. Uptake uses…

exam.q: Explain why low oxygen availability can reduce mineral uptake by roots.
ms: Less oxygen reduces aerobic respiration.
Less energy is available for active transport.
Mineral ions need to move against their concentration gradient.

lessons.title: Organisation and digestion
lessons.summary: Similar cells form tissues, tissues form organs and organs cooperate in systems.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Similar cells form tissues, tissues form organs and organs cooperate in systems. Digestion changes large insoluble molecules into small soluble molecules. Villi provide a large absorbing area and a rich blood supply in the small intestine.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Amylase from salivary glands, pancreas and small intestine breaks starch into sugars. Proteases from stomach, pancreas and small intestine produce amino acids. Lipases from pancreas and small intestine produce glycerol and fatty acids. Liver-made bile is stored in the gall bladder, neutralises acid and emulsifies fat; it is not an enzyme.

keypoints: Similar cells form tissues, tissues form organs and organs cooperate in systems.
Amylase from salivary glands, pancreas and small intestine breaks starch into sugars.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

Where is bile made?

exam.q: Explain how bile assists fat digestion.
ms: It neutralises acid, providing alkaline conditions for lipase.
It emulsifies fat into smaller droplets.
This increases surface area available to lipase.

lessons.title: Enzymes, temperature and pH
lessons.summary: Enzymes are biological catalysts, usually proteins.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Enzymes are biological catalysts, usually proteins. A substrate fits an active site, products are released and the enzyme can be reused. The lock-and-key model explains specificity but is simplified. Catalysts speed reactions without being used up.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Warming initially increases collisions and rate. Above an optimum, active-site shape changes and enzymes denature; extreme pH can do the same. Cold normally slows activity without denaturing. For disappearance of a fixed substrate amount, compare relative rate using 1/time.

keypoints: Enzymes are biological catalysts, usually proteins.
Warming initially increases collisions and rate.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: Starch digestion takes 25 s. Calculate 1/time.
Why is a denatured enzyme less effective?
opts: Its active site no longer fits the substrate
checks.why: Its active site no longer fits the substrate

exam.q: Explain why an enzyme works well at 37°C but poorly at 70°C.
ms: High temperature alters protein structure.
The active site changes shape / denatures.
Fewer substrate molecules fit, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form.

practical.title: Required practical 4 · pH and amylase
method: Equilibrate amylase, starch and buffer at a chosen water-bath temperature.
Mix measured volumes and sample onto iodine every 30 seconds.
Record when iodine no longer turns blue-black; repeat at a range of pH values.
variables: Independent: pH using buffers.
Dependent: time until starch is undetectable, or 1/time.
Control temperature, concentrations, volumes and sampling interval.
safety: Wear eye protection and avoid iodine contact.
Use school-approved amylase rather than saliva.
practical.analysis: Plot mean relative rate against pH. The endpoint lies between the last positive and first negative sample, limiting time resolution to the sampling interval.

lessons.title: Food tests and controls
lessons.summary: Iodine turns blue-black with starch.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Iodine turns blue-black with starch. Heated Benedict’s reagent gives a green to brick-red precipitate with reducing sugars. Biuret turns lilac with protein. Sudan III stains a lipid layer red. Use the correct test conditions; reagent colour alone without the method may mislead.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Use clean separate tubes and droppers, standardised volumes and equal heating time. A known positive checks that the test works; water is a negative control. A negative result means none was detected under those conditions, not proof that absolutely none exists.

keypoints: Iodine turns blue-black with starch.
Use clean separate tubes and droppers, standardised volumes and equal heating time.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: Which indicates protein?
Which test requires a hot water bath?

exam.q: A food turns iodine blue-black but heated Benedict’s stays blue. Interpret the results and name a useful control.
ms: Starch is detected.
Reducing sugar is not detected under the conditions.
A known sugar solution checks the Benedict’s reagent and heating.

practical.title: Required practical 3 · Food tests
method: Prepare similar food suspensions in separate labelled tubes.
Test starch with iodine, reducing sugars with heated Benedict’s and protein with Biuret.
Use the school-approved lipid test, such as Sudan III, and record known positive and water controls.

Control heating duration for Benedict’s comparisons.
safety: Wear eye protection for reagents.

practical.analysis: Record observations separately from conclusions. Negative tests need working positive controls before interpretation.

lessons.title: Heart, vessels and gas exchange
lessons.summary: The right ventricle pumps through the pulmonary artery to lungs; pulmonary veins return blood to the left side.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: The right ventricle pumps through the pulmonary artery to lungs; pulmonary veins return blood to the left side. The left ventricle pumps through the aorta to the body; venae cavae return blood. Coronary arteries supply heart muscle. Valves reduce backflow and a right-atrial pacemaker coordinates rate.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Arteries carry blood away under pressure and have muscular elastic walls. Veins return blood at lower pressure and have valves; thin capillaries permit exchange. Air travels through trachea and bronchi to alveoli, whose large area, thin walls and capillary supply support diffusion.

keypoints: The right ventricle pumps through the pulmonary artery to lungs; pulmonary veins return blood to the left side.
Arteries carry blood away under pressure and have muscular elastic walls.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: Which vessel carries blood to lungs?

exam.q: Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right.
ms: It pumps blood around the whole body.
It must generate a higher pressure.
More muscle produces a greater force of contraction.

lessons.title: Blood and cardiovascular treatments
lessons.summary: Plasma transports dissolved materials including glucose, urea and carbon dioxide.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Plasma transports dissolved materials including glucose, urea and carbon dioxide. Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin and have a biconcave shape and no nucleus. White cells defend against pathogens; platelets help clot blood and reduce blood loss.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Fatty deposits narrow coronary arteries, reducing oxygen supply to heart muscle. Stents hold arteries open; statins reduce blood cholesterol. Replacement valves, pacemakers, donor hearts and temporary artificial hearts address different problems. Compare benefits with procedure risks, side effects and donor availability.

keypoints: Plasma transports dissolved materials including glucose, urea and carbon dioxide.
Fatty deposits narrow coronary arteries, reducing oxygen supply to heart muscle.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

ms: A stent improves blood flow through a narrowed artery.

Heart muscle receives more oxygen for aerobic respiration.

lessons.title: Health, risk factors and cancer
lessons.summary: Health includes physical and mental wellbeing.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Health includes physical and mental wellbeing. Communicable diseases spread between organisms; non-communicable ones do not. Risk factors increase probability, not certainty. Smoking increases lung disease risk; obesity increases type 2 diabetes risk; heavy alcohol use can damage liver tissue.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Correlation alone does not establish causation: age, diet or other confounders may explain an association. Cancer involves uncontrolled division. Benign tumours stay local; malignant tumours invade and can spread to form secondary tumours. Environmental exposure and inherited factors can both influence risk.

keypoints: Health includes physical and mental wellbeing.
Correlation alone does not establish causation: age, diet or other confounders may explain an association.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

lessons.title: Plant tissues and transport
lessons.summary: Palisade cells contain many chloroplasts; spongy mesophyll has air spaces.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Palisade cells contain many chloroplasts; spongy mesophyll has air spaces. Guard cells control stomata. Dead hollow lignified xylem carries water and mineral ions; living phloem translocates dissolved sugars from sources to tissues using or storing them.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Evaporation from leaf cells and diffusion through stomata drive transpiration. Replacement water moves up xylem from roots. Wind and warmth often increase loss; humidity reduces the water-vapour gradient. A potometer estimates water uptake, which differs slightly from transpiration because plants use some water.

keypoints: Palisade cells contain many chloroplasts; spongy mesophyll has air spaces.
Evaporation from leaf cells and diffusion through stomata drive transpiration.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.

lessons.title: Pathogens and named diseases
lessons.summary: Viruses reproduce inside host cells; bacteria can multiply and produce toxins.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Viruses reproduce inside host cells; bacteria can multiply and produce toxins. Measles spreads in droplets, causing fever and rash; HIV damages immune cells and can lead to AIDS. Tobacco mosaic virus causes discoloured leaf areas and reduces photosynthesis.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Salmonella causes food poisoning: hygiene and poultry vaccination reduce transmission. Gonorrhoea is bacterial and sexually transmitted. Rose black spot is fungal. Malaria is caused by a protist carried by mosquitoes: nets and removal of breeding sites reduce transmission.

keypoints: Viruses reproduce inside host cells; bacteria can multiply and produce toxins.
Salmonella causes food poisoning: hygiene and poultry vaccination reduce transmission.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.

lessons.title: Human defences and vaccination
lessons.summary: Skin forms a barrier and clots close wounds.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Skin forms a barrier and clots close wounds. Nose hairs and mucus trap particles; airway cilia move mucus towards the throat. Stomach acid kills many swallowed pathogens. White cells engulf pathogens, make specific antibodies and produce antitoxins.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Vaccines present harmless pathogen antigens and stimulate an immune response. Later exposure triggers faster specific antibody production, often preventing serious illness. High uptake reduces transmission and can protect vulnerable people. Compare rates in comparable populations rather than raw case totals.

keypoints: Skin forms a barrier and clots close wounds.
Vaccines present harmless pathogen antigens and stimulate an immune response.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: What neutralises bacterial toxins?

checks.why: A faster specific immune response occurs

lessons.title: Antibiotics and developing medicines
lessons.summary: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses reproducing inside cells.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses reproducing inside cells. Painkillers relieve symptoms without necessarily destroying pathogens. Penicillin came from mould; aspirin developed from willow chemistry and digitalis from foxgloves. Resistant strains make suitable prescribing important.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Preclinical tests use cells, tissues and animals. Low-dose healthy-volunteer trials examine safety before patient trials assess efficacy and dose. Random allocation and double-blind comparisons reduce bias; a placebo is useful where ethical. Sufficient sample size and peer review strengthen conclusions.

keypoints: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses reproducing inside cells.
Preclinical tests use cells, tissues and animals.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and glucose uses
lessons.summary: Photosynthesis transfers light energy to chemical stores: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Photosynthesis transfers light energy to chemical stores: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen. Chlorophyll absorbs light and the process is endothermic. Recognise CO₂, H₂O, C₆H₁₂O₆ and O₂. Plants respire continuously; photosynthesis needs light.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Glucose supplies respiration and can become starch, oils or cellulose. Nitrate ions supply nitrogen for amino acid and protein synthesis. Insoluble starch is useful for storage because it has little direct osmotic effect compared with an equivalent number of dissolved sugar molecules.

keypoints: Photosynthesis transfers light energy to chemical stores: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.
Glucose supplies respiration and can become starch, oils or cellulose.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: Which gas enters for photosynthesis?

checks.why: For amino acid and protein synthesis

exam.q: Explain three uses of glucose in a growing plant.
ms: Respiration transfers energy for cellular processes.
Cellulose forms cell walls.
Starch or oils store material, or amino acids are made with nitrate-derived nitrogen.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis rate and pondweed
lessons.summary: Light, carbon dioxide, temperature and chlorophyll amount affect photosynthesis.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Light, carbon dioxide, temperature and chlorophyll amount affect photosynthesis. At low light, increasing intensity often raises oxygen production. A horizontal curve shows constant rate rather than no photosynthesis; interpret what the axes actually measure.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Compare oxygen per unit time while controlling plant species and size, carbon dioxide and temperature. Allow equilibration and repeat. Bubble counting is convenient but unequal bubble volumes limit accuracy; gas collection measures volume more directly.

keypoints: Light, carbon dioxide, temperature and chlorophyll amount affect photosynthesis.
Compare oxygen per unit time while controlling plant species and size, carbon dioxide and temperature.
mistakes: Explain the biological mechanism as well as naming it.
Use the conditions and data given; avoid claiming that one observed trend applies in every situation.

checks.q: 18 cm³ oxygen is collected in 6 minutes. Calculate rate.
What does a horizontal oxygen-rate curve indicate?

exam.q: Suggest three improvements to a pondweed experiment comparing light levels.
ms: Control temperature to avoid lamp heating as a confounder.
Keep plant size and carbon dioxide supply consistent.
Collect gas volume over equal periods and repeat for means.

practical.title: Required practical 5 · Light intensity and photosynthesis
method: Place pondweed in bicarbonate solution and arrange oxygen collection.
Change lamp distance or measured intensity, allowing equilibration.
Measure oxygen over a fixed period, repeat and calculate mean rates.
variables: Independent: lamp distance or measured intensity.
Dependent: gas volume per time, or bubble count with its limitation.
Control temperature, carbon dioxide, species and plant size.
safety: Keep electricity away from water.
Handle glass and cutting tools carefully; a cool LED reduces heating.
practical.analysis: Bubble sizes vary, so gas volume is generally a better measure. Control heating separately from light; net oxygen production is influenced by respiration as well as photosynthesis.

lessons.title: Limiting factors and greenhouse economics
lessons.summary: A limiting factor prevents further increase in photosynthesis under the current conditions.

notes.html: A limiting factor prevents further increase in photosynthesis under the current conditions. If extra carbon dioxide raises a plateau, carbon dioxide was limiting there. notes.html: Respiration is an exothermic cellular process supplying energy for movement, synthesis and keeping warm. Aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water. Breathing moves air; it is not respiration. Both plants and animals respire.

lessons.summary: Exercise raises muscular energy demand.

lessons.title: Endocrine glands, insulin and diabetes
lessons.summary: Endocrine glands release hormones into blood; target tissues respond.

notes.html: Endocrine glands release hormones into blood; target tissues respond. Effects are often slower and longer-lasting than nervous responses. Know pituitary, thyroid, adrenals, pancreas, ovaries and testes. Pituitary hormones influence several other glands.

lessons.summary: Low glucose stimulates pancreatic glucagon, causing liver glycogen to become glucose released into blood.

lessons.title: Reproductive hormones and contraception
lessons.summary: Testosterone from testes supports sperm production and male secondary sexual characteristics; ovarian oestrogen supports female development.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Testosterone from testes supports sperm production and male secondary sexual characteristics; ovarian oestrogen supports female development. FSH matures an egg and LH triggers ovulation. Oestrogen and progesterone maintain the uterus lining. Twenty-eight days is a cycle model; real cycle lengths vary.

lessons.summary: FSH stimulates egg maturation and oestrogen secretion.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: FSH stimulates egg maturation and oestrogen secretion. Oestrogen rebuilds the lining, inhibits FSH and stimulates an LH surge. LH causes ovulation; progesterone maintains the lining and inhibits FSH/LH. Falling progesterone allows the lining to break down if pregnancy does not occur.

lessons.title: Reproduction, meiosis and fertilisation
lessons.summary: Sexual reproduction joins gametes and mixes genetic information.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Sexual reproduction joins gametes and mixes genetic information. DNA is replicated once before meiosis, followed by two cell divisions, making four genetically different cells with half the original chromosome number. Human gametes normally have 23 chromosomes; chromosome number is not the same as cell number.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Fertilisation restores paired chromosomes. The zygote grows by mitosis and its cells differentiate. Asexual reproduction has one parent, no gamete fusion and genetically identical offspring apart from mutation. Meiosis creates gametes; mitosis supports growth and asexual reproduction.

keypoints: Sexual reproduction joins gametes and mixes genetic information.

notes.html: DNA is a polymer with two strands forming a double helix. Chromosomes contain DNA; genes are sections coding for amino acid sequences in proteins. A genome is the entire genetic material of an organism. Alleles are versions of genes, not additional organelles.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Genome knowledge can identify disease-associated genes, support research and trace human migration. A variant may increase risk without determining outcome because other genes and environment matter. Evaluate privacy and consent when genetic data are shared.

lessons.title: Alleles, disorders and sex inheritance
lessons.summary: Genotype describes alleles and phenotype describes expressed characteristics.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Genotype describes alleles and phenotype describes expressed characteristics. Homozygous means identical alleles; heterozygous means different alleles. A dominant allele is expressed in a heterozygote. Dominant does not mean more common, stronger or beneficial.

notes.html: Cystic fibrosis uses a recessive inheritance model; polydactyly can be dominant. Interpret pedigrees using the stated symbols and model. In the standard sex-chromosome model, XX is female and XY male; sperm can supply X or Y, giving approximately equal probabilities.

lessons.title: Variation, natural selection and selective breeding
lessons.summary: Variation can be genetic, environmental or both.

exam.q: Why does the graph curve slightly at the start?
ms: The heater has to warm up first, and the thermometer takes time to reach the block's temperature. Energy goes into the heater before it reaches the block, so the first readings rise slowly. Only the straight part is used to find the gradient.

practical.title: Specific heat capacity
method: Measure and record the mass of the metal block (1.00 kg).
Place the immersion heater in the larger hole and the thermometer in the smaller hole. Add a drop of oil to the thermometer hole so the bulb makes good thermal contact.
Wrap the block in an insulating jacket to reduce energy transfer to the surroundings.
Connect the heater to the power supply with an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel across the heater.
Record the starting temperature, then switch on the power supply and start the stopwatch.
Record the temperature, voltmeter and ammeter readings every minute for 10 minutes.
Calculate the energy transferred at each time using E = V × I × t, and plot temperature against energy.
Draw a line of best fit through the straight part of the graph. Specific heat capacity = 1 ÷ (gradient × mass).
variables: Energy transferred to the block (time the heater is on)
Temperature of the block
Mass of the block, material of the block, power supply setting, insulation, starting temperature
safety: The heater and block get very hot. Do not touch them while switched on, and let them cool before packing away.
Place the block on a heat-proof mat.
Keep water away from the electrical equipment.
Use a low-voltage supply only, and switch off before changing connections.

practical.title: Resistance
method: Attach a length of constantan wire to a metre rule with tape at each end.
Connect a cell, switch and ammeter in series with the wire, using crocodile clips on the wire. Clip the first one at the 0 cm mark.
Connect a voltmeter across the wire between the two crocodile clips.
Place the second crocodile clip 10 cm from the first. Close the switch, record the ammeter and voltmeter readings, then open the switch.
Move the clip in 10 cm steps up to 100 cm, recording the readings at each length.
Calculate the resistance at each length using R = V ÷ I and plot resistance against length.
For the second part, connect two resistors in series, then in parallel. Measure V and I for each arrangement and calculate the total resistance.
variables: Length of wire (or the arrangement of resistors)
Resistance, calculated from the potential difference and current
Material and diameter of the wire, temperature of the wire, the cell used
safety: The wire can get hot if the current is large, particularly at short lengths. Open the switch between readings and do not touch the wire while current flows.
Never connect the crocodile clips together directly, as this short-circuits the cell.

practical.title: Density
method: Regular solid: measure the mass on a digital balance. Measure the length, width and height with digital calipers (or a ruler). Volume = length × width × height.
Irregular solid: measure the mass. Fill a eureka can with water until it drips from the spout, then wait until it stops. Place an empty measuring cylinder under the spout.
Lower the object into the can on a thread. Read the volume of displaced water in the measuring cylinder at eye level, from the bottom of the meniscus. This equals the volume of the object.
Liquid: place an empty measuring cylinder on the balance and press tare (zero). Pour in a measured volume of liquid and record the mass.
Calculate the density using ρ = m ÷ V. Repeat and find a mean.

Mass and volume (used to calculate density)
Temperature, how the meniscus is read, the same balance
safety: Wipe up spilled water immediately to avoid slips.
Lower objects gently into the eureka can so the water does not splash.
Ethanol is flammable. Keep it away from flames.

practical.title: Force and extension
method: Clamp the spring to a clamp stand and clamp a metre rule vertically beside it, with its zero at the top.
Fix a pointer (a splint) to the bottom of the spring so it lies horizontally against the rule.
Record the pointer reading with no load. This is the starting position.
Hang the 100 g mass hanger on the spring. Wait for it to stop moving, then record the pointer reading at eye level.
Add 100 g slotted masses one at a time, recording the reading after each.
Calculate the extension each time: extension = reading − starting reading. Calculate the weight: W = m × g.
Plot force (y-axis) against extension (x-axis). The gradient of the straight section is the spring constant k.
variables: Force on the spring (weight of the masses)
Extension of the spring
The same spring throughout, the same position on the pointer, reading at eye level
safety: Wear eye protection in case the spring snaps or flies off.
Clamp the stand to the bench, or use a heavy base, so it cannot topple.
Do not stand with your feet under the masses. Put a soft tray beneath them in case they fall.

practical.title: Acceleration
method: Clamp a pulley to the end of the bench. Attach a string to the trolley, pass it over the pulley and tie it to a mass hanger.
Fix a card of known length (5.0 cm) on top of the trolley. Set up two light gates so the card passes through both, and connect them to a data logger.
Tilt the runway slightly so the trolley just keeps moving at a steady speed when pushed. This compensates for friction.
To vary the force: put five 20 g masses on the system. Move masses one at a time from the trolley to the hanger, so the total mass being accelerated stays the same.
Release the trolley from the same place each time. Record the time for the card to pass each gate and the time between the gates.
Calculate each speed (v = card length ÷ time at gate) and the acceleration a = (v₂ − v₁) ÷ t.
To vary the mass: keep the hanging mass the same and add masses to the trolley.
Plot acceleration against force, and acceleration against 1 ÷ mass.
variables: Resultant force (or mass)
Acceleration
Mass of the system (or the force), card length, gate positions, the slope of the runway
safety: Place a box of padding where the masses land so they do not hit your feet or the floor.
Put a buffer at the end of the runway to stop the trolley.
Keep feet and hands clear of the falling masses.

practical.title: Waves
method: Ripple tank: set up the tank with about 1 cm of water, a lamp above it and a sheet of white paper underneath. Use a straight dipper connected to a signal generator.
Switch on and adjust the frequency until you can see clear wave shadows on the paper. Record the frequency from the signal generator.
Place a ruler on the paper. Measure across as many waves as possible (for example 10) and divide by the number of waves to find the wavelength. A photo of the pattern makes this easier.
Calculate the wave speed with v = f × λ. Repeat for different frequencies.
Waves on a string: attach a string to a vibration generator, pass it over a pulley and hang masses on the end to keep it taut.
Switch on the signal generator and adjust the frequency until a clear standing wave appears.
Measure the length of a whole number of half wavelengths (loops) with a metre rule. Wavelength = 2 × length ÷ number of loops.
Calculate the speed using v = f × λ.
variables: Frequency of the signal generator
Wavelength
Depth of water (ripple tank); tension and type of string (string)
safety: Keep the water in the ripple tank well away from the electrical supply to the lamp.

method: Place the Leslie cube on a heat-proof mat. Fill it with very hot water from a kettle and put the lid on.
